clue.text: At which the gun in hand is worth one bird in the bush ?

definitions.text: At which the gun in hand is worth one bird in the bush ?

parts.words: At which the gun in hand is worth one bird in the bush
parts.note: the proverb says a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, so a gun worth only one is worth half a bird, half a male bird, and a gun can be held at that safety position

explanation.surface: A twist on the proverb about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush, with a gun in place of the bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A gun at half-cock has its hammer raised halfway, where it cannot fire; the proverb's halving of the bird's value gives half a cock.
explanation.definitionFit: Half-cock is the safety position of a gun's hammer, partly raised but locked.

clue.text: Rustic deity in a classic way is one for the birds

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: via is the Latin, classical, word for way or road
a faun is a Roman god of the countryside, half man and half goat

explanation.surface: A country god on an ancient road is a friend to birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classic' points to Latin: the classical word for a road. 'one for the birds' sounds dismissive but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the collective term for all the bird life of a region.

clue.text: Old man river

parts.note: an old man, a parent, is father
the Thames is the river of London

explanation.surface: An old man personifying a river, as in the song.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Thames is the traditional personification of London's river, pictured as an old bearded man.
explanation.definitionFit: The river Thames is personified as an old bearded man in statues and verse.

clue.text: We need a bishop to measure how long the road

parts.note: Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, was William the Conqueror's half-brother
a meter is a measuring instrument

explanation.surface: We need a bishop to survey the length of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Odo was the Norman bishop of Bayeux; METER is a measurer, as in gas meter. The device records how long the road travelled was.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument in a car records distance travelled, telling how long the road was.

clue.text: Christopher's about ten — Tom's much younger

indicators.note: one piece goes about, surrounding, the other

parts.note: Kit is the short form of Christopher, so Christopher's is Kit's

explanation.surface: Christopher is about ten years old, and Tom is much younger.
explanation.walkthrough: Kit is the usual pet form of Christopher. 'Tom' looks like a second boy, but a tom is a male cat, so its much younger ones are its young.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, and its young are baby cats.

clue.text: Carriage from Germany

parts.note: a four-wheeled carriage with a folding top, named after a town in the Palatinate where it was first made

explanation.surface: A carriage imported from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The carriage takes its name from the German town of Landau.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-wheeled horse-drawn coach with a two-part folding hood, named after its German town of origin.

clue.text: Panic in evidence as the aircraft descends

definitions.meaning: a panic or fuss, as in 'getting in a state'

definitions.text: in evidence as the aircraft descends
definitions.meaning: the hinged sections of a wing are lowered when a plane comes in to land

explanation.surface: Passengers panic as the plane comes down.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of agitation is a panic; the hinged wing sections lowered for landing share the name.

clue.text: Chicken state

parts.note: a fried chicken dish bears the name of an American state on Chesapeake Bay

explanation.surface: A cowardly nation, or a state of fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' suggests cowardice, but the dish chicken Maryland is fried chicken named after the US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state on Chesapeake Bay that gives its name to a fried chicken dish.

clue.text: She appears as Belial in disguise

indicators.note: something in disguise is made to look different, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman is the devil Belial dressed up as someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disguise' rearranges the letters of AS BELIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella is a woman's name, so it can stand for any 'she'.

clue.text: Roll to port perhaps

definitions.meaning: a roll is a register of names
a ship that leans over to one side, port for example, is said to do this

explanation.surface: A ship rolls over towards its port side.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is a register, as in a class roll; a ship leaning to one side, perhaps the port side, is tilting that way.

clue.text: Nearly an all-round master of words

definitions.text: Nearly an all-round master of words

parts.words: Nearly an all-round master of words
parts.note: the egg-shaped character of the nursery rhyme is nearly round, and in Through the Looking-Glass he insists words mean what he chooses, asking who is to be master

explanation.surface: Praise for a near-perfect, versatile wordsmith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All-round' looks like 'versatile' but means shaped almost like a ball: an egg. In Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass this egg says of words, 'The question is which is to be master'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's egg-shaped character claims mastery over what his words mean.

clue.text: O stay and rest thy weary head upon this breast — from the back benches ?

definitions.text: O stay and rest thy weary head upon this breast — from the back benches ?

parts.words: O stay and rest thy weary head upon this breast — from the back benches
parts.note: a young unmarried woman's tender words, and also a new member's first address to Parliament from the back benches

explanation.surface: A romantic plea, oddly heard in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted line is what a young woman might say to a lover; an MP's first address to the House of Commons, usually made from the back benches, is called by the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: A new Member of Parliament's first speech in the House is given this name; read literally, it is a young woman's words.

clue.text: It was caught in a light noose

definitions.text: It was caught in a light noose

parts.words: It was caught in a light noose
parts.note: a quotation from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, where the Hunter of the East catches the Sultan's tower top in a noose of light at dawn

explanation.surface: Something got snared in a flimsy loop of rope.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening of FitzGerald's Rubaiyat: 'And Lo! the Hunter of the East has caught / The Sultan's Turret in a Noose of Light.' A 'light noose' is the first sunlight, not a flimsy rope.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem, dawn sunlight catches the top of the Sultan's tower, a small tower on a building.

clue.text: Phaeacian princess lost her ball but found Odysseus

definitions.text: Phaeacian princess lost her ball but found Odysseus

parts.words: Phaeacian princess lost her ball but found Odysseus
parts.note: in Homer's Odyssey, the daughter of King Alcinous plays ball on the shore; the ball falls into the river and the shouting wakes the shipwrecked hero

explanation.surface: A princess loses a ball game but finds a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: In Odyssey Book 6 the Phaeacian princess's ball goes astray while she plays with her maids, and their cry wakes Odysseus, who is hiding in the bushes.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the daughter of the Phaeacian king Alcinous, who meets the shipwrecked Odysseus.

clue.text: Lady-killers who broke down King Edward ?

definitions.meaning: dandies who chase women were called by this slang word around 1900
King Edward is a potato variety, and kitchen tools that break potatoes down into a purée are called this

explanation.surface: Womanisers who brought down the king.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is a British potato variety, named after Edward VII; the tool that pulps potatoes shares a name with Edwardian ladies' men.
explanation.definitionFit: Late Victorian and Edwardian slang for flashy men who flirt with women; also kitchen tools that pulp cooked potatoes.

clue.text: Wonder man — wander man?

parts.note: a worker of wonders, and one of the Magi, the wise men from the East who wandered following the star

explanation.surface: A marvellous man, or one who roams.
explanation.walkthrough: A worker of wonders is a conjuror, and the word also suggests one of the Magi who travelled to Bethlehem.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror works wonders; the Magi were the wise men who wandered to Bethlehem.

clue.text: Dashed round the tee, getting saturated

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: dashed means sped, moved fast
taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer races around the tee box and gets soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashed' looks like disappointed but means raced; 'the tee' is the golf tee, given as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Something soaked in liquid until it is full of it is wholly saturated.

clue.text: A censer made of bone in the furthest island

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Thule, Ultima Thule, was the classical name for the northernmost island of the known world
a rib is a bone

explanation.surface: An incense burner carved from bone on a remote island.
explanation.walkthrough: Ultima Thule was the Roman name for the most northerly land, imagined as an island at the world's edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging metal vessel used to burn incense in church services.

clue.text: Colman for President! — little matter

parts.note: a campaign slogan urges voters to elect someone to the office
Ronald Colman was a British film star, Ron for short

explanation.surface: A campaign slogan backing a film star for President, a trivial matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Colman was a British-born Hollywood actor of the 1930s and 40s. 'little matter' reads as 'trifle' but is a tiny particle of matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny subatomic particle, a very small piece of matter.

clue.text: Scottish island for example upset, but put in order

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A Scottish island is upset, but someone tidies it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns EG into GE.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange things is to set them out in a proper sequence.

clue.text: Euclidean caterpillar?

parts.note: a student of Euclid measures the earth, and so does the looper caterpillar of a moth family that seems to measure the ground as it moves

explanation.surface: A caterpillar with a taste for geometry.
explanation.walkthrough: The looper caterpillars of one moth family arch and stretch as if measuring the ground, which gives the family its name, the same as a word for a practitioner of Euclid's subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a geometrician, like Euclid, and a looper moth or its caterpillar.

clue.text: The vessel holds one example of scholastic work

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: one piece holds, contains, the other

parts.note: SS is the steamship prefix, so a vessel
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A ship carries one sample of academic writing.
explanation.walkthrough: SS is the usual crossword vessel, from the steamship prefix; 'example of' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissertation written for a university degree is a piece of academic work.

clue.text: Land of the red hand

parts.note: the Red Hand is the emblem of the northern Irish province, from the legend of a chief who cut off his hand to claim the land

explanation.surface: A country stained with blood.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Hand of Ulster is the heraldic badge of the province of Ulster, in the north of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern province of Ireland has a red hand on its flag.

clue.text: X test reveals a variety of Mexican roses

indicators.note: a variety of things is a mix of them, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A test reveals a new strain of rose from Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X test' reads as X for cross and test for examine. 'a variety of' rearranges MEXICAN ROSES.
explanation.definitionFit: X is a cross and test means examine, so the pair spells out questioning a witness for the other side.

clue.text: Capital that turned Napoleon's head ?

annotationWithheld.why: Capital that turned Napoleon's head ? (4): no parse found for OSLO; 'turned Napoleon's head' gives no letters that make OSLO, and no source gives the setter's reading

clue.text: Country that is turned about

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the letters for 'that is' are read backwards

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
re is Latin for about, concerning

explanation.surface: A nation that has done an about-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' gives EI from IE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eire is the Irish-language name for Ireland, a country.

clue.text: Giving the O.K. to a definition of "sundry debtors"

definitions.meaning: split into two words, all of them in debt: everyone has something to pay

explanation.surface: An accountant approves a definition of one balance-sheet item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a definition of' joins the two definitions. Sundry debtors are the miscellaneous people who owe a business money: split into two words the answer says they all owe.
explanation.definitionFit: Permitting means approving; split as two words the answer says everyone owes, describing a list of people in debt.

clue.text: " He thought he saw an — That practised on a fife " (Carroll)

definitions.text: He thought he saw an — That practised on a fife " (Carroll)

parts.words: He thought he saw an — That practised on a fife
parts.note: lines from the Mad Gardener's Song in Lewis Carroll's Sylvie and Bruno; the missing word is the beast he thought he saw

explanation.surface: A line of Carroll's nonsense verse with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mad Gardener's Song opens: 'He thought he saw an Elephant, / That practised on a fife: / He looked again, and found it was / A letter from his wife.'
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's mad gardener mistakes a letter from his wife for a large tusked beast playing a fife.
